slides.title: The operating system most servers run
points: Almost every cloud server and container runs Linux. Working comfortably in its shell is the base skill for operations work.
Everything is a file or a process, and small tools combine through pipes.

slides.title: Processes, files, permissions, services
points: Processes: ps, top, kill; each has a PID, an owner and limits.
Files and permissions: owner, group, others; read, write, execute; root can do anything, so avoid working as root.
Services run under systemd (systemctl status, journalctl -u for logs).
Pipes chain tools: grep, awk, sort, uniq, tail -f turn logs into answers.

slides.title: Power and sharp edges
points: A single command can delete everything; check paths, especially with rm -rf and variables.
Changes made by hand on a server are lost or forgotten; write them as code (see infrastructure as code).
Distributions differ (Debian/Ubuntu apt, Red Hat dnf), in package names and paths.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Disk full: df -h, then du to find what grew (often logs).
High load: top, then which process, then why.
SSH keys, not passwords, and sudo for the few commands that need root.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: How requests find your servers
points: Every request crosses DNS, IP routing, ports, TLS and usually a load balancer before reaching your code.
Most 'the site is down' incidents are a broken link in that chain.

slides.title: IP, ports, DNS, balancers
points: IP addresses identify machines; ports identify services on them (443 for HTTPS); private networks (10.x, 192.168.x) aren't reachable from the internet.
TCP gives reliable ordered connections; UDP is lighter and unordered.
DNS maps names to addresses; records are cached for their TTL, so changes take time to spread.
Load balancers spread traffic across healthy servers and remove ones failing health checks.

slides.title: Layers to debug
points: Firewalls and security groups block by default; a missing rule looks like a timeout.
Long DNS TTLs reduce lookups and slow down emergency changes.
Layer 4 balancers are fast and simple; layer 7 balancers can route by path and header.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: dig or nslookup for DNS; curl -v for the whole request; nc or telnet to test a port.
A timeout usually means something blocked or nothing listening; 'connection refused' means the host answered and nothing listens on that port.
Lower the DNS TTL a day before planned changes.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Automating the boring parts
points: Scripts in Bash or Python automate repeated tasks: deployments, backups, clean-ups, checks.
A task done by hand twice is a candidate for a script.

slides.title: Safe scripts
points: In Bash, start with set -euo pipefail so errors stop the script instead of continuing silently.
Quote variables ("$file") so spaces don't split them.
Python is better once there's logic, data parsing or an API to call.
Make scripts idempotent: running twice does no harm.

slides.title: Quick script or real tool
points: Bash is everywhere and fast to write, and gets unreadable past a page.
A script that only one person understands is a risk; keep it in version control with a short usage note.
Hard-coded secrets in scripts leak; read them from the environment or a secrets manager.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A --dry-run flag that shows what would change.
Logs of what the script did, with timestamps.
shellcheck run on every Bash script.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Running containers at scale
points: Kubernetes runs containers across a cluster of machines, keeping the number you asked for running and replacing ones that fail.
You describe the desired state; Kubernetes works to make reality match.

slides.title: Pods, deployments, services
points: A pod is one or more containers scheduled together on a node.
A deployment keeps N replicas of a pod running and rolls out new versions gradually.
A service gives pods a stable address and load-balances between them; an ingress routes outside traffic in.
Liveness and readiness probes tell Kubernetes when to restart a container and when to send it traffic.

slides.title: Powerful and heavy
points: Kubernetes is a lot to run and learn; a managed service (EKS, GKE, AKS) or a simpler platform may be enough.
Resource requests and limits must be set, or pods get evicted or starve neighbours.
YAML grows fast; templates (Helm, Kustomize) help and add their own complexity.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: kubectl get pods, describe, logs: the first three commands in any incident.
CrashLoopBackOff: the container keeps exiting; read its logs and recent changes.
Rolling updates with readiness probes, so traffic only reaches pods that are ready.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Servers and networks written as code
points: Infrastructure as code (IaC) describes cloud resources in files (Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation) that a tool applies.
The same review, history and repeatability you have for application code, applied to infrastructure.

slides.title: Declare, plan, apply
points: You declare what should exist; the tool compares it with what does and plans the changes.
Always read the plan before applying: it shows what will be created, changed or destroyed.
State records what the tool manages; keep it remote, locked and backed up.
Modules package repeated patterns (a standard service, a network).

slides.title: Discipline pays, drift hurts
points: Changes made by hand in the console drift from the code and get overwritten or cause surprises.
Some changes replace a resource (destroy and recreate); the plan says so, so read it.
Very large single configurations get slow and risky; split by area.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Plans posted on pull requests; applies run from CI, not laptops.
Separate environments (staging, production) with the same modules.
Prevent-destroy protection on databases and storage.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: From commit to production, automatically
points: Continuous integration builds and tests every change; continuous delivery makes every passing change ready to deploy, and continuous deployment ships it.
The goal is small, frequent, boring releases.

slides.title: Build once, promote
points: Every push runs the pipeline: build, test, scan, package.
Build one artifact (an image) and promote that same artifact through staging to production.
Deploy gradually (canary, blue-green) with automatic rollback on bad health.
Pipelines are code, kept with the application.

slides.title: Speed against safety
points: Long pipelines slow everyone down; cache dependencies and run tests in parallel.
Flaky tests erode trust in the pipeline; fix or quarantine them.
Secrets in pipelines are a favourite target; scope and rotate them.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins or a cloud service.
Main always deployable; changes merged small and often.
Deployment frequency and change failure rate tracked (DORA metrics).

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: The services every cloud offers
points: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud offer the same core pieces under different names: compute, storage, networking, databases and identity.
Knowing the categories transfers between providers.

slides.title: Compute, storage, identity
points: Compute: virtual machines (EC2), containers (ECS, GKE), functions (Lambda) — less to manage as you go right, and less control.
Storage: object storage (S3) for files, block storage for disks, managed databases for data.
Networking: virtual private clouds, subnets, security groups, load balancers.
Identity (IAM): who or what may do which action on which resource; roles for services, not long-lived keys.

slides.title: Managed or self-run
points: Managed services save operations work and cost more per unit, and tie you to the provider.
Serverless scales to zero and has cold starts and limits.
Everything is billed by use; forgotten resources cost money forever.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Accounts or projects separated by environment.
Tags on every resource for cost and ownership.
No access keys on laptops; short-lived credentials through single sign-on.

points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: A server's application stops writing logs and errors say 'No space left on device'. What do you check first?
choices: df -h to see which filesystem is full, then du to find what grew (often old logs), and set up log rotation
why: Find what filled the disk, free it, and stop it recurring.
It may come back up full.
Memory isn't disk.
The disk is still full.

newQuestions.stem: A new service is unreachable: curl to its port hangs until it times out, but the process is running and listening. What's the likeliest cause?
choices: A firewall or security group isn't allowing traffic to that port
The service is listening on the wrong port number
why: A silent drop (hang then timeout) points at a firewall; a wrong port usually gives 'connection refused'.
DNS would give the wrong address or fail to resolve.
That usually gives an immediate refusal.
TLS errors appear after connecting.

newQuestions.stem: A Bash clean-up script runs `rm -rf $DIR/*`. One day DIR is empty because an earlier command failed. What happens, and what prevents it?
choices: It deletes from / (the root); use set -euo pipefail, quote variables, and check DIR is set (for example ${DIR:?})
Nothing; an empty variable is skipped
why: An empty $DIR turns the path into /*; failing fast and guarding the variable stop it.
Bash expands it to an empty string.
DIR is empty, so there's no DIR in the path.
rm -rf never asks.

newQuestions.stem: During a rolling update, users get errors for a few seconds as each new pod starts. What's usually missing?
choices: A readiness probe, so traffic goes to a pod only once it can serve
More replicas of the old version
why: Without readiness, Kubernetes sends traffic as soon as the container starts.
It doesn't stop traffic reaching unready pods.
Size isn't the issue.
Liveness decides restarts, not traffic.

newQuestions.stem: A Terraform plan for a small change shows the production database will be 'destroyed and recreated'. What do you do?
choices: Stop: find which attribute forces replacement, change the approach (or protect the resource), and never apply a plan that destroys data unexpectedly
why: Replacement of a database loses its data; the plan is warning you.
The tool does what the code says, not what you meant.
Timing doesn't save the data.
That makes Terraform forget what it manages, which is worse.

newQuestions.stem: Staging passes, but production behaves differently because the image was rebuilt for production with newer dependencies. What principle fixes this?
choices: Build once and promote the same artifact through every environment
why: The thing tested is the thing shipped.
That moves the risk to users.
Two rebuilds can differ in the same way.
That's the cause.

newQuestions.stem: An application on a cloud VM needs to read one storage bucket. How should it get access?
choices: Attach a role to the VM that allows reading only that bucket
Put an administrator's access key in the app's config file
why: Short-lived role credentials with least privilege; no keys to leak.
A leaked admin key compromises everything.
Anyone could read the data.
Not how cloud access works, and unsafe.
